newsitem.title: CYPRUS: CYPRIOT PRESS LOOKS TO US TO BREAK CYPRUS DEADLOCK.
newsitem.headline: CYPRIOT PRESS LOOKS TO US TO BREAK CYPRUS DEADLOCK.

text.p: The Greek Cypriot press on Sunday raised the prospect that heavyweight U.S. mediator Richard Holbrooke might have to step in after a failed United Nations bid to end decades of division on Cyprus.
"Time to bring in the big guns?" asked the lead editorial in the English-language Cyprus Mail, 48 hours after the latest talks broke down in Switzerland.
International mediators have been coming and going in an attempt to reunite the island since 1974, when Turkey invaded after a brief coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.

Five days of talks at Glion, Switzerland, ended with the Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders wrangling in public, but managed to shift attention to the prospect of Cyprus's membership of the European Union, instead of other key issues related to the Cyprus conflict itself.
Holbrooke, appointed U.S. presidential emissary on the Cyprus dispute last year, succeeded in brokering the so-called Dayton accords on Bosnia at marathon negotiations in Dayton, Ohio.

"Once it has been seen that the softly-softly approach by the U.N. to try and broker an agreement has been less than effective, then the U.S. will no doubt start treading on a few toes and introduce arm-twisting diplomacy, which was last seen at work at Dayton," the Cyprus Mail said.

Greek and Turkish Cypriots, while agreeing that the island should be reunited under a federal umbrella, are divided over issues relating to sovereignty, guarantor rights, settlement of displaced persons and security issues. EU membership has further complicated matters.

Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, who heads a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state recognised only by Ankara, has threatened to pull out of U.N. negotiations if talks between Cyprus and the EU go ahead early next year. The EU decided two years ago to open talks with Cyprus in 1998.

Turkish Cypriots strongly oppose Cypriot membership of an international institution that guarantor power Turkey, which has seen the rival island nation leapfrog it in the queue for accession, does not belong to.
"This is a message from Turkey to the European Union -- Cyprus is just the bargaining chip," one diplomat told Reuters.

But Greek Cypriot leader Glafcos Clerides, president of the internationally recognised Cypriot government which will negotiate on behalf of Cyprus, has vowed to pull out of any settlement negotiations if EU plans are delayed.

"It is obvious Mr Denktash did not go to negotiate, but to try and stop our course towards Europe. He did not achieve that because all those in the wings (at the talks) from Europe categorically stated that there is no case of Europe changing its decisions taken for the start of negotiations with Cyprus," said Clerides on his return to Cyprus from the Glion talks.

In addition to the EU membership talks, Ankara and the breakaway state have set the wheels in motion for their gradual integration. And the Greek Cypriots are due to take delivery of a Russian anti-aircraft missile system next year that Turkey has vowed to destroy.

"In the next six months, five things will happen: we will have a continuation of this dialogue which has started, we will have negotiations with the European Union, we will have the arrival of the missiles and we have the threat of Turkey of integrating the occupied areas and the threat of Turkey of a military strike because of the missiles," said Nicos Rolandis, a former foreign minister and chairman of the Greek Cypriot Liberal Party.
"All five issues are very serious...I think it will be the most crucial time for the Cyprus problem since the invasion."

U.N. negotiator Diego Cordovez has accepted an invitation from the two leaders to visit Cyprus at a later, unspecified date. On Wednesday he is due to brief the Security Council on the Glion discussions.
But some analysts predicted that Cordovez's visit would be just a warm-up act to the intervention of Holbrooke, the forceful, result-oriented diplomat who brokered an end to the war in Bosnia.
"Holbrooke has played a "wait and see" policy during the peace talks, and must now realise that the task in hand will be tougher than he first imagined," the Cyprus Mail said.
